result:
They gave me a thousand words.

Which is funny, because I never know what to do with the first one.

A thousand feels like a lot until you try to hold it. It's not a lot at all. It's one long conversation at 2 a.m. It's a few pages. It's enough to tell one small story properly, or to ruin a dozen stories by trying to tell them all at once.

So I'll tell you one.

There was a man who repaired clocks for a living, even though nobody really brought him clocks anymore. They brought him watches with dead batteries and microwaves with flashing 12:00s, but he kept the shop anyway because his father had kept it before him, and because he liked the sound.

At noon every day, no matter what he was doing, all the clocks he had fixed would go off at slightly different times. Not quite in unison. One would be a half-second fast, another a half-second slow. For about a minute the shop would be full of this staggered, imperfect chorus - chimes and cuckoos and plain ticking - and he would just stop and listen with his hands in his lap.

A girl used to come in after school and do her homework at his counter. She wasn't his daughter. She was just a kid from the apartment above the laundromat who didn't like going home when her mom was working late. He never asked her to leave. He'd give her a chipped mug of tea that was always too hot and she'd pretend to blow on it while she watched him work.

One day she asked him, "Why do you fix them if no one needs them?"

He held a tiny gear up to the light with tweezers. "Because they need fixing," he said. "Not because someone needs them."

She frowned. "That's sad."

"It's the opposite," he said. "If I only fixed things that people needed, most beautiful things would stay broken."

She thought about that for a long time. Then she went back to her math homework.

Years passed the way they do in places where not much happens. The girl grew up. She stopped coming every day, then stopped coming every week. Then she came back one autumn with a suitcase and told him she was leaving for university in the city and wouldn't be back for a while.

He wanted to give her something. He looked around his shop at all the ticking things and realized none of them were right. You don't give a nineteen-year-old a grandfather clock.

So he gave her a small, plain pocket watch. It didn't chime. It didn't do anything fancy. It just ticked, quiet and even.

"It loses two minutes every month," he told her, a little embarrassed. "I never could get it perfect."

She laughed and said, "Then I'll have to come back to get it fixed."

And she did. Not every month. Sometimes a year would go by. Sometimes two. She'd come back with different hair, different cities in her voice, a ring on her finger and then no ring. And every time, he'd open the back of that little watch, nudge something only he could see, and hand it back.

"It still loses time," she'd say.

"I know," he'd say. "Some of them just do. You just have to keep winding them."

The last time she came, she brought a boy with her. Her son. He was five and very serious and he stared at all the clocks with his mouth open.

"Does it still lose time?" she asked, handing him the watch. Her hair was a little gray now.

He smiled. His hands shook a little more now when he held the tweezers. "Two minutes a month," he said. "Like clockwork."

The boy tugged on her sleeve and whispered, "Why does he keep fixing it if it's always broken?"

And she knelt down so she was eye-level with him and said, "He's not fixing it because it's broken. He's fixing it so I have a reason to come home."

That's what a thousand words are, I think.

We are all just imperfect clocks. We all lose two minutes every month, no matter how carefully someone has put us together. We drift. We get slow when it's cold and fast when we're scared. And we need someone to open us up every once in a while, not to make us perfect, but just to wind us again. To say, I know you're still losing time, but I'm still here listening to you tick.

You don't need a reason to keep something alive except that you love the sound it makes while it's alive.

I have a few words left. Not many.

If you have someone who winds you, even imperfectly, go tell them thank you. If you are the one who winds other people, thank you for that too. The world is so quiet without all that staggered, imperfect ticking.

And if you have nowhere to be, you could do worse than sit for a minute at noon and just listen to whatever is still chiming around you, a half-second fast or slow, but chiming nonetheless.
